canonicalExplanation.summary: Integrating a PR happens after review: **address feedback with new commits**, reply to each comment, and get **re-review** of what changed. Then the project's policy decides the button. **Merge commit** keeps every commit plus a merge marker. **Squash** combines the branch into one commit on main. **Rebase** replays each commit linearly. The same final code can produce very different history, so follow the policy. Crucially, **checks must pass on the exact head being merged**: a green tick from before your last push doesn't count. Afterwards, verify main and delete the merged branch.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.body:
A learner's PR has eight commits like "wip", "typo" and "fix review". Tests passed yesterday; this morning they pushed one more tweak and want to merge before CI finishes. A squash policy combines a noisy feature history into one target commit only after current required checks pass on the reviewed head. In this lesson you'll revise, re-review and integrate a pull request while preserving traceability.

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.body: You should know **Remotes and synchronization**, **Code review** (blockers and re-review) and **Conflict resolution** (combining both intents).

sections.heading: The rule: current checks, approved head, policy button
sections.body:
```bash
# Address review feedback with focused commits.
git commit -m "Guard empty cart in total()"
git push                                  # reply to each comment; request re-review.

gh pr checks 61                           # all required checks green on this head?
gh pr merge 61 --squash --delete-branch   # the project's policy: squash.

git switch main && git pull --ff-only
git log --oneline -3                      # one commit: "Fix empty cart total (#61)".
npm test                                  # verify main itself.
```

| Policy | Main's history | Good for |
|---|---|---|
| merge commit. | all branch commits + merge. | keeping full detail. |
| squash. | one commit per PR. | noisy branches, simple history. |
| rebase. | branch commits, linear. | clean, meaningful commits. |

```reveal
{"prompt": "How does a squashed commit stay traceable?", "answer": "Its message includes the PR number, and the PR page keeps the full discussion and original commits. Edit the squash message to summarise the change, not list \"wip\" and \"typo\"."}
```

examples.title: Squashing a noisy feature
examples.situation: A squash policy combines a noisy feature history into one target commit only after current required checks pass on the reviewed head.
walkthrough: **Noisy feature history:** eight commits including "wip" and "typo" on the branch.
**Current required checks pass on the reviewed head:** the learner waits for CI on today's commit to turn green and re-review to approve.
**A squash policy combines them into one target commit:** main gains "Fix empty cart total (#61)"; git log will show a single clean entry.
examples.result: Main's history stays readable, and the PR page keeps the full story.

examples.title: The stale green tick
examples.situation: A PR was approved with passing checks. The author then merged main into it to resolve a conflict and clicked merge immediately. Main's build broke.
walkthrough: The conflict resolution created new code nobody tested.
Required checks should have run again on the new head.
Branch protection can enforce "checks must pass on latest commit".
examples.result: After enabling that rule, every merge is tested exactly as it lands.

misconceptions.mistakenBelief: Any merge button produces equivalent history and a green check from an earlier commit remains valid after new changes.
misconceptions.correction: Merge, squash and rebase give different histories, so the project's policy matters. And checks only prove the commit they ran on; any new push needs new checks.
misconceptions.diagnosticPrompt: In "The stale green tick", why did main's build break?

analogy.example: Integrating is like **publishing an edited article**. Changes from the editor are made and re-checked (re-review), the final proof is checked again after the last edit (current checks), and the house style decides whether drafts are kept or folded into one clean version (policy).
limitations: Articles rarely break other articles; merges can break main.
The drafts stay in the archive (the PR page).
